articles.title_orig: France's Macron tightens curbs on protests, blaming hard left for unrest
articles.title_zh: France's Macron tightens curbs on protests, blaming hard left for unrest
articles.content_orig:
French authorities have barred demonstrations in several of the country’s largest cities, as President Emmanuel Macron blamed far-left groups for stoking violence during weekend protests .
The Paris Police Prefecture announced that Thursday’s protests would be banned in key parts of the city until 8pm (18:00 GMT). That includes areas near the presidential Elysee Palace, both houses of parliament, the city’s main train stations, as well as parts of downtown where looting occurred over the weekend.
A police source told the AFP news agency the ban was necessary due to organisers’ “inability to prevent violence and vandalism”.
Elsewhere in France, authorities also prohibited protests planned for Thursday in Lyon, Lille and Grenoble.
The restrictions come after more than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday in a protest that brought together students demanding better conditions in schools and groups denouncing high living costs. At least 2,500 people were arrested after riots broke out in several areas , with shops looted.
French President Emmanuel Macron blamed Saturday’s riots on what he called “seditious acts” by “ultra-left” groups, whom he accused of trying to “bring down the Republic”.
Speaking from the Elysee Palace on Thursday, Macron said France would ban all “illegitimate” protests in the coming days, while approved demonstrations led by organised groups like unions would be required to take alternative routes outside city centres to protect businesses .
He added that he would convene the country’s defence council on Friday to take further action.
Thursday’s planned protests were seen as a prelude to a large demonstration on Saturday, when activists from the “yellow vest” movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, are expected to join.
Some of those protests, including marches in Lyon, will also be banned, local authorities said.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who met union representatives on Wednesday, said a “massive” security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures.
Meanwhile, Macron held a meeting with intelligence services, Lecornu and ministers on Thursday morning to obtain a detailed account of what went wrong over the weekend and review preparations for upcoming protests.
Union representatives said their meeting with Lecornu did not result in concrete proposals. They are now focusing on another big day of action scheduled for November 5, calling on private and public sector employees to join.
The education demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school in Creteil, southeast of Paris, over a lack of staff.
From there, class strikes, blockades and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide, including in smaller towns.
High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods.
The school demonstrations and blockades have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs.

articles.content_orig:
Meta shares slumped roughly 6% on Thursday as the social media giant showed negative free cash flow in its third-quarter earnings and raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditures.
The spread on the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs on Thursday, a signal of growing credit concerns from investors as the company leans deeper into its artificial intelligence spending plans.
Meta said it expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from a previous $130 billion to $145 billion.
Free cash flow came in at a negative $2.12 billion during the quarter.
The company revealed Wednesday that it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock during its earnings release, meant to maintain its "founder-led structure" and "provide Meta the ability to finance its growth."
Meta also said CEO Mark Zuckerberg could leave the state if the "California Wealth Tax" were to pass, as he "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion-dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company," according to the SEC filing.
Zuckerberg was convinced to stay in California with the company's new stock plan, the filing noted.
Revenue for the social media giant jumped 26% in the third quarter from a year ago, coming in at $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. Earnings per share were reported at $3.83, though it wasn't clear if it was directly comparable to the $5.75 per share Wall Street was looking for.
—CNBC's Jonathan Vanian and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

It seems to be the question many in the energy markets are asking. We are about to enter the ninth month of the Iran war. Or Iran "conflict." At this point, it's not very clear what to call it. The only thing right now that's "clear" is that very little is clear.
Oil is moving through the Strait of Hormuz. Most Gulf nation export volumes are well up from their lows. Iran volumes are the exception. Those are down to the point of almost being nonexistent. From the little information that trickles out of the mostly closed country, it seems the Iranian economy is crumbling. Iran's currency is losing value, and people I speak with who have family there tell me they are increasingly worried about more economic pain ahead.
Iran has one main source of money: oil. Without oil, there is little money. Without money, there is little ability to buy the weapons, drones, and missiles that cause havoc and spread fear in the Gulf. Iran is going to grow more desperate, which makes Iran even more dangerous. In just the last week or so, multiple ships have been attacked. Iran's proxy gang - the Yemeni terror group known as the Houthis - has recently killed civilians in Saudi Arabia with attacks on the airport. They also blew up part of Aramco's headquarters.
The point is this is not just a grim recap of where we stand, but an attempt to understand where we're going. As I've said and written before… I have no idea. I'm not sure that anyone really does. The best we can do is gather as much information and intelligence as possible and make educated guesses. Sorry to say it, but right now, guessing is what many are doing. The markets remain one good or bad headline away from a $10 move in oil in either direction.
While we wait, oil markets stay elevated. The paper price of oil is around $100 per barrel. Most companies and countries don't use "paper" oil. As I wrote last week , the price of an actual physical barrel of oil is much, much higher than what you see on your screens. In some cases, it may be double.
Another of the few things we are clear on is that demand destruction is not here yet. All prices are up, and demand is staying relatively consistent. Sky-high diesel prices across Europe are going to hit demand, but they have not landed a knockout blow yet. $100 oil and $10 diesel are not what they used to be. Inflation has been a huge part of the global economic story since COVID and the lockdowns. Those were self-imposed, and I would argue that this is as well, because the attacks on Iran — whether you believe them to be just, given that regime's cruelty toward its own people — were a human decision. Humans got us into this, and humans are going to have to get us out.
It doesn't appear that we are any closer to a real resolution than we were a few months ago. Shipping costs continue to soar, and insurance is available but expensive.
What now is that we keep as calm as we can and carry on. Every week, I write Power Insider knowing tomorrow could be an entirely different headline. But like it or not, oil is the lifeblood of the global economy. And it will be for decades to come. So the oil must flow. And it is flowing. But at a cost.
Meantime, global markets wait for any scrap of clarity. What little we have will come from corporate earnings and any guidance management can provide. Energy services firm SLB (SLB) is first out of the gate with numbers on October 23. Baker Hughes (BKR) and natural gas exporter Cheniere Energy (LNG) are next. But the real focus comes on October 30, when both ExxonMobil (XOM) and Chevron (CVX) show off their earnings. It's not rocket science knowing those numbers will be big. Sales will rise with the price of oil. Refining earnings will be even bigger. The biggest piece of news, however, will be whatever glimmer of guidance these companies feel confident enough to provide. My spider sense tells me it won't be much. While mega oil and gas companies pay for some of the greatest intelligence in the world, even the world's greatest intelligence gatherers are subject to the whims of rogues with missile launchers.
Thanks for reading—and watching—and be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

Neil has loved the refining stocks for a while — a great call — but is now turning his focus to other names. He hasn't fallen out of love with the refiners; it's just that so much money has been made that he feels there are better opportunities elsewhere. Here are a few.
On the large-cap side, he loves two companies with new CEOs: ConocoPhillips (COP) and Occidental Petroleum (OXY) .
Conoco's legendary boss, Ryan Lance, has made way for Andrew O'Brien. Neil doesn't see that as a problem, but is watching two things closely: COP's huge new Willow project in Alaska and the status of the damaged natural gas plant at QatarEnergy, in which ConocoPhillips is invested.
Occidental also has a new CEO, Richard Jackson, and Goldman recently upgraded the stock to Buy from Neutral with a $69 target. More bullishly, Goldman chose to add OXY to its vaunted "America's Conviction List." The company has long been saddled with high debt, but it's pushing through a new plan to improve cash flow. Investors have been rewarded with a solid 53% gain over the last year, but Neil Mehta sees more to come.

The group largely trades with the price of crude, so if we do get a meaningful peace with Iran — a big "if," I know — oil prices are likely to drop, perhaps meaningfully. I look forward to hopefully speaking soon with the CEOs of both ConocoPhillips and Occidental Petroleum about all of this and more.
Those two are the megacaps. I'd like to now hit on two of the smaller-cap, less-talked-about stocks on Goldman's golden list.

articles.title_zh: Amex Platinum adds Airbnb perks and credits, ends one-night hotel credits
articles.content_orig:
American Express is bringing Airbnb into its travel rewards platform.
The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring more than 1 million Airbnb listings to Amex's travel portal and allow cardholders to earn rewards when booking the stays. It does not currently allow members to redeem points to pay for Airbnb bookings.
The launch adds Airbnb rentals to Amex's hotel portfolio, which includes more than 3,400 properties across its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection programs.
Amex members with either the consumer or business Platinum card can also now apply their $600 annual lodging credit — previously called the hotel credit — to Airbnb's higher-end Luxe stays and take advantage of a new $250 statement credit on eligible Airbnb Experiences after making a Luxe booking.
"We're excited to bring more choice and flexibility to American Express Card Members with this exclusive partnership. Both of our companies exist to help people travel more and better, and this partnership helps people see more of the world by making travel more rewarding," said Juan David Borrero, head of partnerships at Airbnb, in a news release.

The changes come as competition among premium credit cards continues to ramp up.
Last year, American Express raised the annual fee on its premium Platinum card to $895. In turn, it's been investing in cardholder perks such as new lounges in airports and at big-ticket events and experiences as a way to attract more high-paying customers.
Earlier this month, it announced an expansion of its Centurion Lounges , with renovations coming to four existing lounges and new ones planned for Newark Liberty International Airport and London Heathrow Airport. The Newark lounge will be the largest in its network.
The partnership also comes as Americans continue to opt for travel and luxury experiences, even as prices for airfare, gas and hotels rise. Despite higher costs, more than half of Americans reported making no changes to their travel plans this summer , a recent study by travel insurance company Squaremouth found.

articles.title_orig: Cruise lines chase luxury travelers with suites for up to $25,000 a night
articles.title_zh: Cruise lines chase luxury travelers with suites for up to $25,000 a night
articles.content_orig:
The latest push into high-end travel is taking place on the high seas, as cruise lines increasingly lean on luxury offerings.
On Regent's Seven Seas Splendor, an all-luxury ship, cabins cost anywhere from $1,800 to $15,000 per night for its top-of-the-line booking, the Regent Suite.
The difference is not just the roughly 5,100 square feet of space. The top-tier suite has a Steinway piano, a private dining room reserved for its occupants, and a wraparound deck with a hot tub and a view comparable to the one from the ship's bridge.
Multiple passengers wanted the suite for Splendor’s 151-night global cruise that embarks in January, Regent told CNBC, and it is almost always occupied.
Regent is setting its sights even bigger, as the cruise line plans to debut Seven Seas Prestige in December, its first new ship class in a decade. Its top suite costs $25,000 per night.
While mega-ships with surfing and water slides can carry more than 7,500 passengers, the smaller, elite ships — some carrying fewer than a thousand passengers — are powering profits for companies like Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings . The company owns luxury lines Regent and Oceania.
Norwegian CEO John Chidsey has said he's focused on sharpening the luxury brands' positioning, improving the products and guest experience, and strengthening their commercial performance.
Regent and Oceania, he said, are in good shape for 2027, though Chidsey did not break out metrics between the companies.
Cruise competitors are also betting big on luxury offerings, investing in new ships and more specialized experiences.
Regent competes with established luxury cruise lines including Royal Caribbean's Silversea and Carnival's Seabourn, as well as newer entrants carrying hotel names into the market. Four Seasons, Aman and Orient Express are among the brands bringing luxury hospitality to yacht-style vessels.
The cruise industry projects the luxury cruise fleet will grow from 104 ships in 2026 to at least 130 by 2036.
And while global cruise passengers are forecast to increase about 11% between 2025 and 2028, according to the Cruise Lines International Association, or CLIA, the industry's investment dollars are increasingly flowing to luxury and expedition brands, with orders rising for smaller ships and fewer berths through the next decade.
From 2020 through 2025, there has been a 71% increase in the number of luxury ships and an 84% increase in berths, according to CLIA. The orders indicate another 26% jump in number of ships through the end of 2029 and a 32% increase in capacity.
Other hospitality companies are investing and expanding their uber-upscale offerings, too. Hotels, casinos, airlines, restaurants, spas and other travel and leisure companies see the trend: Affluent customers remain willing to pay for more space , personal service and distinctive experiences.
United Airlines this year launched its larger Polaris Studio suites with privacy doors and caviar service. American Airlines increased its lie-flat capacity and reported on Thursday that its premium passenger unit revenue rose 18.5% in the third quarter, compared with 14.4% in its main cabin.
Marriott’s second-quarter results showed luxury revenue per available room growing faster than the broader hotel business in the U.S. and Canada, rising 9.1% year over year, compared with 5% for all Marriott hotels in the region. In June, CEO Anthony Capuano told CNBC there's an “almost insatiable appetite” for luxury travel.
Wynn Resorts, which caters almost exclusively to high-end customers, has opted to maintain its high room rates in Las Vegas even as visitation has slowed over the past year, rather than filling every room with travelers looking for a bargain.
Asked onstage at the Global Gaming Expo in September whether Wynn is extracting more profit from fewer customers, CEO Craig Billings said, "We will always focus on what's the most comfortable experience for the customer and where can we drive the highest possible EBITDA."
But offering luxury vacations doesn't guarantee a company's fortunes.
The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, for instance, has struggled with occupancy despite major marketing campaigns and has accumulated nearly $700 million in losses since 2017, according to the Financial Times.
More competition in the space could undercut the perception of scarcity. As more companies add luxury products, they have to convince travelers that the experience is worth the price.
Las Vegas Sands reported earnings Wednesday that missed expectations for revenue and profit, hurt by the high-end segments in both Macao and Singapore.
"When the customers don't show up, it's a little problematic," CEO Patrick Dumont said on the company's  earnings call.
Dumont said he couldn't point to any single cause for the softness, adding, "perhaps people are not feeling as good about the market," but he said he believes this quarter is an aberration.
CNBC asked Dumont during the NBA China Games in Macao on Oct. 9 whether luxury travel could become overcrowded.
In response, he pointed to the long-term wealth creation in Asia and said the challenge was making experiences customers want to return to.
“It’s not about, are there enough customers,” he said. “It’s, can we create enough of an interesting set of experiences where people find us indispensable in their lives.”

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
articles.content_orig:
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.
The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.
Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials , though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network.
However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, which occurred after he spoke with administration officials multiple times seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, according to sources familiar with the situation.
There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.
Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.
On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News .
Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.
Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.
Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.
The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.
It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters .
Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.
In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.
Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.
On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.
CBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed.
Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, sources said. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.
The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.
The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that."
Musk has not admitted to imposing restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X .
He added that Starlink is a "commercial service," writing that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."
Rubio, however, seemed to attribute the network constraints to Musk.
"The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.
Within a few minutes, though, he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used.  Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."
At around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.

Warhammer Tone Pro: Superb coverage and vibrant colours
The Warhammer Tone Pro range lands on the shelf on Saturday. Yesterday, we saw just how flexible the new paints are , and today we’re looking at their coverage and vibrancy.
One of the first things you’ll notice when you open a pot of Tone Pro is how smooth and consistent the paint is, and all 150 paints have the same consistency. Then, when you’ve got the paint onto your brush, you’ll feel how smoothly it flows onto your miniatures.
The paints give incredible coverage – it’s the best coverage so far from a Warhammer paint. Even white* and yellow, which are notoriously difficult colours to get right, give a solid, opaque coat from the first application. The quality of the pigment in the paint is what allows it to cover so well, and it makes painting even those notorious colours much more accessible.
It’s not just the coverage, Tone Pro also has some of the most vibrant colours of Warhammer paints too. This really opens up your options for creativity and the different stories you can tell with your miniatures. They also work really well with the existing Warhammer Colour range, opening up even more options for your colour schemes.
Finally, the new paints will self-level as they dry. This means you’ll get a really smooth finish, brush strokes will disappear, and the details on your miniatures don’t get clogged up. This makes Tone Pro both easy to use and incredibly forgiving.
You’ll be able to get your hands on the new paints from Saturday. Head down to your local store to begin a new era of Warhammer painting.

articles.title_orig: Mark Zuckerberg threatened to leave California over proposed billionaire tax, Meta says
articles.title_zh: Mark Zuckerberg threatened to leave California over proposed billionaire tax, Meta says
articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg threatened to move out of California if residents of the state approve a first-of-its-kind billionaire wealth tax when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3, the company said in a new regulatory filing .
Because of his concerns over the wealth tax, Zuckerberg told Meta that he was "evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and that steps toward any such relocation, including any listing of his residential real estate in California on the market, would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees and, accordingly, raise questions for management of the company going forward," the filing states.
Meta said that because Zuckerberg's presence near the company's Menlo Park, California, headquarters is "critically important" to its success, the company took an unusual step: Its board approved a new class of nonvoting common stock that he can sell to raise cash to pay the wealth tax, if voters approve it.
Without that change, Zuckerberg faced the prospect of having to sell voting shares to raise funds to pay the tax, which would have reduced his control of Meta.
As a result of that decision to issue new stock, Zuckerberg has told Meta he will commit to remaining a California resident for eight years. If Meta moves its headquarters to another state, Zuckerberg will move to that jurisdiction, according to the regulatory filing.
The disclosure highlights the public debate over the proposed billionaire wealth tax, known as Proposition 40, which will be on the Nov. 3 ballot in California. Under the proposal, the tax would impose a one-time 5% state tax on billionaire wealth — about $12.4 billion of Zuckerberg's estimated $247 billion net worth, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.
The company believes "it is critically important to keep Mr. Zuckerberg in a leadership position with our company and that he continue to reside in and manage the company from our headquarters in California to ensure his continued ability to effectively drive our performance during this era of unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry," Meta said in its filing.
The billionaire tax is aimed at raising $100 billion from the state's wealthiest residents, with the money earmarked for shoring up California's healthcare system. Stanford University economists have questioned whether the tax could backfire, given that several billionaires have already moved out of the state. The economists said that could result in lower projected wealth taxes and reduced overall income tax collections.
Creating a new stock class isn't only designed to keep Zuckerberg near Meta's headquarters, according to the filing.
The publicly listed, nonvoting Class C common stock, which will become effective in January, is also intended in part to boost the company's ability to raise capital for AI infrastructure investments. It will also use the new stock to raise capital, compensate employees, make acquisitions and for other general corporate purposes.
"Meta plans to issue nonvoting shares to fund AI investments without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control," said Andrew Rocco, stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
articles.content_orig:
Accommodation platform acts after long-standing guest complaints over doing dishes, taking out rubbish and stripping beds
Airbnb hosts will no longer be able to ask guests to strip beds or wash dishes under the accommodation platform’s new rules.
The changes, which apply to Airbnb reservations covered by the platform’s global policy, will come into effect on 20 November and limit chores imposed on guests.
Airbnb had long fielded complaints from guests about having to pay cleaning fees, which can be hundreds of dollars, and still complete a list of chores for their host.
Since April 2025, cleaning fees have not been shown to guests. Instead, hosts have been allowed to choose to factor cleaning costs into the total price of the stay.
In a community policy update posted on its website this week, Airbnb said hosts would “generally” no longer be allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that “require significant effort or time or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
Examples of such tasks include stripping beds of linen, taking rubbish offsite, and washing and putting away dishes, the company said.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules which must be displayed in full at the time of booking – and can also add other “reasonable” requests.
Examples of house rules include check in and check out times, limits on how many guests can stay at the property, smoking restrictions, quiet hours, and whether or not pets are allowed.
Reasonable requests depend on “relevant local considerations”. For example, it may be reasonable to ask guests to limit shower time due to local water restrictions, or to dispose of rubbish in an animal-proof container.
after newsletter promotion
While guests shouldn’t be asked to wash and put away dishes under the new guidelines, hosts can ask them to put used dishes in the sink.
“House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage,” an Airbnb spokesperson said.
“So we’ve redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”

articles.title_orig: ‘Gears Of War: E-Day’ Cost Xbox $500 Million, Says New Report
articles.title_zh: ‘Gears Of War: E-Day’ Cost Xbox $500 Million, Says New Report
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive Games Gears Of War: E-Day PS5 The Coalition Xbox
Gears of War: E-Day is a terrific game and it has the highest Metacritic score of any entry in the franchise since the original Xbox 360 trilogy. But early estimates suggest the positive buzz has not resulted in blockbuster sales numbers. That makes it an interesting test case for Xbox’s return to exclusivity, especially for a game that cost so much.
The first rumors of Gears of War: E-Day ‘s budget arose in June after it was shown during Xbox’s summer showcase. Insider Gaming ‘s Tom Henderson said at the time he’d heard the cost to ship the shooter was “insane” and over $400 million. Windows Central ‘s Jez Corden pushed back on that claim. He suggested the budget was lower and that accounting for the cost of The Coalition is tricky because of the work the studio does supporting teams across Xbox Game Studios.
But according to one source familiar with Xbox’s business, the cost of Gears of War: E-Day is in fact much higher. They told Kotaku it was over $500 million, and that’s before you include marketing. That would put it significantly above the reported budgets of other console-exclusive blockbusters this generation , like Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 . E-Day would need to sell millions and millions of copies across all platforms to make up the difference. Microsoft did not respond to a request for comment.
Current forecasts suggest E-Day ‘s nowhere close. Alinea Analytics estimated the game sold 230,000 copies in its first week and generated just $37 million in revenue, a big chunk of which came from Game Pass subscribers paying $30 for the Premium Edition Upgrade to unlock early access. These numbers will have gone up in the two weeks since launch, but the initial momentum points to a money hole too deep for any multiplatform frag grenade to close. According to the source, E-Day was unlikely to recoup its costs no matter which platforms it came to, but as a console exclusive it could contribute to rebuilding user activity on Xbox in key areas.
Microsoft hasn’t released official metrics for E-Day ‘s performance yet, unlike it did shortly after Gears 5 released back in 2019. That entry brought in over 3 million players at launch. “The performance easily doubled the first week’s debut of Gears of War 4 and made Gears 5 the most-played Xbox Game Studios title in its first week since 2012’s Halo 4 ,” the company wrote in a press release at the time. It has so far stayed quiet on how many people have played E-Day .
Would this math have meaningfully changed if Microsoft hadn’t chosen to pull the game from PlayStation 5? It seems unlikely. Earlier this year, Alinea Analytics estimated that Gears of War: Reloaded , a remaster of the first game in the franchise and the first Gears to ever appear on PlayStation, sold 684,000 copies on PS5. Selling that many copies of E-Day on PS5 would have translated to roughly $33 million in additional revenue after subtracting Sony’s standard platform fees.
It’s possible that a well-reviewed new entry would have made an even bigger splash on PlayStation, though how much bigger is hard to tell. Reloaded was only $40 while E-Day is $70. E-Day is estimated to have sold fewer than 100,000 copies on Steam so far, though it is also available through Game Pass on PC. But no matter how you slice it, the math will not get you anywhere close to $500 million. E-Day seems poised to be a catastrophic miss for Xbox Game Studios in that regard, and an indictment of an Xbox business and game development strategy for an entire console generation.
That same math is also potentially why Xbox console exclusivity for E-Day could end up yielding greater benefits for the platform in the long run than just a few tens of millions in additional revenue. The knock-on effects are harder to measure but more significant to Xbox’s long-term health. As a big fall exclusive on Xbox, E-Day can build buzz, give some players who haven’t turned on their old Xbox Series X/S in a while a reason to come back, and potentially nudge overall engagement on the platform up in a holiday period when players are making lots of choices about what games to buy and what platforms to buy them on.
All of that could end up being worth more than a few hundred thousand additional sales on PS5. Perhaps that’s also why Forza Horizon 6 still hasn’t arrived on Sony’s console. Originally due out on PS5 sometime in 2026, the hit open-world racer’s multiplatform release has been delayed until January 2027 . Why put one of the best-selling games of the year on PS5 right as people are deciding where to buy the biggest releases of the year: Madden , EA Sports FC , NBA 2K27 , Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , and Grand Theft Auto 6 ?
That’s one argument for turning a $500 million game that will seemingly never make its money back into an Xbox Series X/S console exclusive . A recently leaked Xbox Insider survey that suggested the company is looking at leaning even further into reversing course on the recent multiplatform pivot. It was aimed specifically at users with multiple devices and trying to gain insight into how their playing habits would change under different scenarios.
“Imagine it was announced that all future title releases from every Xbox-developed gaming franchise except Call of Duty will be console-exclusive to Xbox,” the final survey question reads . “For Minecraft only, existing titles would no longer be available for purchase on PlayStation or Nintendo consoles, and would not receive any new content updates. However, there is no impact to any of the existing titles or content you already own. Nothing changes on PC in this announcement.”
It asks users what they would do in this situation: turn on the Xbox console they already own, buy a new one, switch to PC, or skip the game entirely. The feedback to questions like these could further cement Xbox’s shift back toward exclusive content. One section of the survey even hints at the possibility for franchises like The Elder Scrolls and Fallout to become console exclusives. It’s unclear where games like The Elder Scrolls 6 and Diablo 5 will end up in the future, but for now Xbox has told its players to “expect signature exclusives from us every year.”
One thing that does seem certain is that sooner or later, Xbox will need to pick a lane and stop swerving into oncoming traffic. Ex-PlayStation executive Shawn Layden called it the company’s “ Dreamcast moment .” “Either you’re going to be a platform competitive with PlayStation, which Xbox has not been competitive with PlayStation for years, but that’s not out the window,” he said last month. “You know, you can still make another run at it. And there are certain decisions you have to make around that about the platform.”
He continued, “We talked about exclusivity. We talked about, how do you incentivize third parties to support your platform in a meaningful way? This is all things around the platform business. Or you sit back and realize you are the biggest game publisher in the world.”

articles.title_zh: Tesla stock slips despite Q3 earnings beat, better-than-expected capex spend
articles.content_orig:

Tesla ( TSLA ) reported better-than-expected third quarter earnings, with its free cash flow and capex spending coming in ahead of Wall Street estimates.
Tesla reported Q3 revenue of $28.05 billion vs. Bloomberg consensus of $28.13 billion. Tesla posted adjusted EPS of $0.48 vs. the $0.44 estimate, with adjusted EBITDA of $3.90 billion vs. $3.66 billion.
Tesla stock pared some of its earlier losses, with Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein claiming the market was reacting to "capacity constraints in the company's auto and battery growth, which could slow near-term growth."
But that might not be the whole story. Tesla reported free cash flow of $1.53 billion vs. an estimated -$4.92 billion, with capital expenditures climbing to $4.732 billion vs. an estimated $7.96 billion for the quarter.
On the earnings call, Tesla updated its full-year capex guidance to $20 billion from $25 billion previously. Tesla CFO Vaibhav Taneja said the savings would come from "managing our capital deployment efficiently, and plan to fund [capex] primarily from our cash flows from operations," he said.
"I think capex is actually ending up being a little lower than we anticipated, but we'll start to become more meaningful next year. And then noticeable in the tens of billions in '28," CEO Elon Musk said on the call.
Roundhill CEO Dave Mazza posits the cutting capex means the Tesla isn't transitioning fast enough to an AI-focused company betting on robotaxis, Optimus robots, and compute.
Tesla revealed its Optimus robot started production at its Fremont factory. "While we will continue to iterate on the hardware and manufacturing process, we have proven that the current manufacturing process for Optimus is suitable for a commercial product," the company said in its earnings release.
"I would expect that it takes us probably at least a year — maybe a little longer — to get to that annualized rate [1 million units], to get to 20,000 units a week," Musk said on the earnings call. Musk added that Tesla may release an Optimus demo video in about a month, stressing that he didn't want the robot's movements to be preplanned.
Regarding its other AI efforts, Tesla said it plans to reach 400 MW of AI training compute by the end of the year. Tesla said its active FSD (full self-driving) subscriptions climbed to 1.74 million.
"The biggest driver of demand is full self-driving," Musk said regarding vehicle sales.
"The Cybercab fleet in Austin has grown by a factor of 10," Musk added while discussing Tesla's robotaxi fleet. He added, "I don't think there's any company in the world that can match our scale with autonomous vehicles."
Musk also stirred the pot recently with comments about a possible tie-up with SpaceX, his other company.
"I think both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss this idea," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call Tuesday night. "At the request of shareholders, and these special committees consist of independent directors. And because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions of the special committees."
He added , "I don't think we should necessarily assume that I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty. And I think that would be overstating it. Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes."
On the Tesla call, Musk briefly touched on it but added nothing new. "With regard to a potential merger with SpaceX, I think I said everything that should be said yesterday [Tuesday]," Musk said.

Tesla began commercial Cybercab service in Austin on Sept. 3, but federal regulators have questions. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) issued Tesla a special order with 21 requests on how it self-certified the Cybercab, which has no steering wheel or pedals, as compliant with federal safety standards. Tesla asked for an extension to Nov. 20. NHTSA granted 30 days instead , making answers due Oct. 30.
Tesla also finally revealed its long-delayed Roadster last Thursday at SpaceX's ( SPCX ) facility in Waco, Texas. The car used cold-gas thrusters to jump over several Teslas, including a Semi. Tesla said the Roadster hit 0-60 mph in 0.81 seconds in a test at the event, and Musk said production starts in 2028.
Deepwater's Gene Munster called it an "engineering flex" with little commercial value, and Morningstar expects the Roadster to sell fewer than 2,000 units a year.

articles.title_orig: Tests show Pope Leo XIV won’t need further treatment for lung cancer, Vatican says
articles.title_zh: Tests show Pope Leo XIV won’t need further treatment for lung cancer, Vatican says
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer surgery last week was a success, and no further treatment is required, the Vatican press office said in a bulletin Wednesday.
“The final histological reports and molecular biology analyses of the tissue removed during the Holy Father’s surgery have been completed today,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the pope’s personal physician, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, a thoracic surgery professor who led the surgical team.
“The results have confirmed that the condition was a pulmonary adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the bulletin added.
Pulmonary adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, accounting for roughly 40% of all cases. It’s slow-moving and often affects nonsmokers.
Leo’s announcement on October 11 that he required surgery for a “nodule” on his lung came as a shock both within and outside the Vatican, given the pope’s penchant for clean living. After a short stay at a hospital in Rome, where doctors removed the lobe of his right lung, Leo returned home on October 17.
The next day, he made his first public appearance since his diagnosis, leading the Sunday Angelus from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace.
“This experience has given me a profound sense of closeness to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity,” he told crowds of worshipers.
Pope Leo’s recovery has beeen much faster than normal, according to Dr. Juanita Mora, the national medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association, who was not part of his care team. She said doctors will monitor the pope after his recent treatment, including follow-up CT scans every three to six months for the first few years, then annually to check for any regrowth.
After such surgery, patients often have respiratory physiotherapy to restore breathing capacity, Mora told CNN, adding that his affected lung should regain full function.
The all-clear arrives ahead of the pontiff’s planned South America trip next month. The news that the pope had cancer complicated plans for the journey, scheduled to include stops in Peru, Uruguay and Argentina and require at least 14 flights.
Though the Vatican has not officially confirmed the pope’s plans for travel, Margaritora, his surgeon, told Vatican News that he saw “no clinical reasons” for canceling the trip.
If the trip goes ahead, the pontiff will probably be told to walk during his travels to prevent blood clots that can form during long flights, according to Mora. The pope, she said, should get Covid-19, flu and RSV vaccines ahead of his trip for “a little extra protection in case he were to get any of the respiratory infections.”
CNN’s Sharon Braithwaite and Jen Christensen contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: COROS DURA 2 SOLAR Review: Big Upgrade, Bigger Price
articles.content_orig:
The latest race content, interviews, features, reviews and expert buying guides, direct to your inbox!
Your newsletter sign-up was successful
Coros has launched the new Dura 2 Solar bike computer today, in what is a major update to the brand's original Dura model, which launched in 2024.
The original Dura made waves when it launched thanks to its solar charging technology, which provided at least a 120-hour battery life, making the unit popular with long-distance riders or those who wanted to cut down on regular charging.
The Dura 2 Solar maintains the same claimed 120-hour battery life from a single charge, not including solar power and 2:1 solar regeneration (meaning you gain two hours of battery for every hour of sun exposure) that the original unit had, and there's been a major overhaul everywhere else.
The unit has been redesigned into a slicker, lighter package; the old digital dial is gone, and the hardware has been given a major upgrade.
In short, the Dura 2 Solar seems to be a far more premium overall package that looks more capable of taking the fight to the big hitters when it comes to the best bike computers .
Something else that has changed is the price: the Dura 2 has a retail price of $499 / £429 / €499, a healthy amount more than the previous unit's RRP of $249 and comes without a mount.
The unit uses a horizontal quarter-turn standard (Garmin mount), and the brand argues most riders already have a mount, or need a specific one anyway for their bike's handlebars.
The latest race content, interviews, features, reviews and expert buying guides, direct to your inbox!
A computer and mount option is available for $549 / £479 / €549, and standard and out-front mounts are available for $79 / £69 / €79.
The unit will be available for purchase from the 27th of October. We understand the original Coros Dura unit will be phased out from this point.
We have everything we know so far here on the computer, as well as our first impressions after logging some rides with the new unit.
The Dura 2 Solar looks radically different to the outgoing unit; it's now lighter than before at a claimed 99 grams and uses a T700 carbon fibre backplate and aluminium alloy in its construction.
The front half of the unit is incredibly thin at just 5.7mm, whilst the solar charging panels have been moved to the bottom of the computer. There are two buttons on either side of the computer body, as well as a USB-C charging port on the right-hand side. There are also two new haptic buttons which can be found on the solar panel as well.
The screen is now bigger; the Dura 2 has a 3.5" Sharp MIP (memory-in-pixel) colour touchscreen, an increase over the old unit's 2.7" screen. Coros has provided some details. The screen has a 17:9 aspect ratio and 201 pixels per square inch.
Like the Garmin Edge 1060 computer that launched this week, the Dura 2 also has a voice control feature. Pressing both buttons on the side of the unit activates the voice control feature, which can be toggled on and off.
The unit, as you might expect, is WiFi, ANT+, and Bluetooth-friendly and works with GPS, GLONASS, GALILEO, BDS and QZSS satellite systems. The brand promises improved routing, pinch-to-zoom screen mapping, climb alerts, and offline re-routing.
Routes can be built in the Coros companion app, which also supports a workout planner and training metric analytics features.
There's also a built-in bike bell, media and camera control functionality, and the ability to upload to ChatGPT and Claude for training analysis.
Shimano and SRAM drivetrain support is built in, and Coros says Campagnolo compatibility will come at the end of the year. Third-party app connections can also be made to the likes of Zwift, Wahoo, Strava, Ride with GPS, Komoot, TrainingPeaks and TrainerRoad.
I've been riding with the Dura 2 for a little while and have logged five hours on the unit so far. Aesthetically, it looks pretty cool, sleek and thoroughly modern, the very thin-to-normal body design perhaps looks slightly disjointed, but that's being really picky.
On the lack of a mount coming with the unit, I see no issue. Most riders will have a Garmin-type mount already, and may likely have their own bike specific out-front mounts sorted anyway. It's one less mount in the spares box in my eyes.
After my initial shakedown ride, I fully charged the Dura 2 and, to test the battery, will use it without recharging until I need to.
After five hours of riding and five days of use, I am at 92.9% battery, with a 0.9% solar charge. You can put the unit into sleep mode in about three seconds, or fully turn it off; I've left it asleep for days at a time.
I've been riding with the screen brightness on full, and with PM and HRM sensors paired, for context. It seems safe to say the battery life is considerably bigger than anything else on the market, like the previous unit.
Initially, at unboxing, I was left disappointed by the unit's screen brightness and overall resolution, noting it to be not as vivid or bright as the Karoo or premium Garmin models. In use, this has been less of an issue than I thought it would be, and outdoors on max screen brightness, the screen is perfectly acceptable to me.
The unit is also fast, one of my colleague Josh's key complaints regarding the original Dura was that it was a touch laggy. The touchscreen is very fast and simple to use, as is the overall user interface and processing speed; no issues from me there.
The map layout looks very good, clearer than Garmin units for me, and up there with the best units around. I'm yet to fully test the navigation features, though.
My only other minor issues at this point are that I can't quite figure out how to get my main road activity profile exactly as I want it, and the lap notification screen takes too long to get rid of, but those things will get answered in time.
I'm already grinning at not having to plug the thing in or check the battery, and the unit is proving to be very capable; it also looks darn pretty cool mounted on your bars. Watch this space for a full review.

articles.title_orig: Barclays to Cut 5,000 Jobs in A.I.-Driven Push to Lower Costs
articles.title_zh: Barclays to Cut 5,000 Jobs in A.I.-Driven Push to Lower Costs
articles.content_orig:
By ANGHARAD CARRICK, BUSINESS NEWS EDITOR and PATRICK TOOHER, CONSULTANT CITY EDITOR
Updated: 10:50 EDT, 22 October 2026
Barclays will cut 5,000 jobs by the end of this year as it pushes to replace staff with artificial intelligence.
The lender, which reported another profit surge last quarter, said there had already been 1,000 roles axed, with a further 4,000 planned.
The job losses form part of a growing shift in the banking sector towards AI in a bid to cut costs.
And it comes after HSBC was this month reported to have been readying for a 'brutal' jobs cull in its wealth management division.
Barclays, which is nearing the end of a three-year cost-cutting drive, said the move would prune 5 per cent of its global workforce.
‘We employ AI at scale but AI is the icing on the cake, it is not the cake,’ Barclays chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan, who is known as Venkat, told analysts.
Barclays expects to make ‘efficiency savings’ of at least £1.1billion next year, with Venkat vowing he would ‘drive hard’ at realising more gains from adopting AI.
It is unclear how many of the 5,000 full-time job cuts will be in the UK, but 3,000 of them will be in ‘support’ roles, including software developers.
Barclays CEO CS Venkatakrishnan said AI had been the 'icing on the cake'
Venkat also highlighted how technology had reduced online mortgage application times from 45 minutes to 15 minutes and meant 10 per cent fewer staff were needed in each bank branch.
‘These little things go a long way,’ he added.
Union Unite described the job cuts as a 'short-term, kneejerk approach,' adding it was 'working with its members to find the best way forward to reset this destructive announcement.'
The lender reported another boost in profits in the third quarter, with plans to hand out more cash to investors ahead of a tax raid on banks in next week’s Budget .
Barclays posted a 12 per cent rise in pre-tax profits to £2.3billion for the three months to September 30, compared to £2.1billion a year earlier.
But the results were overshadowed by the looming windfall tax on bank profits in Chancellor John Healey’s first Budget on Wednesday.
The biggest banks, including Barclays, pay a 3 per cent surcharge above the 25 per cent corporation tax rate.
This is expected to increase to 8 per cent under Healey’s plans to bring in an extra £2billion a year to the Treasury.
Industry figures have warned it will hit investment and growth, pushing up mortgage rates in the process.
Barclays' boss has previously pleaded with the Treasury to leave the bank levy at its current level, telling reporters that ‘for every £1 of capital we have, we lend £8 to £10’ to businesses and households that supports economic growth.
This morning, Barclays also revealed plans for a new £500million share buyback, bringing distributions so far this year to £2.8billion, up 46 per cent year-on-year.
Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trade Union Congress, said: ‘Barclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly.
'All the big banks are doing exceptionally well at the same time – but their windfall profits have been underpinned by mortgage misery for millions. That’s why it’s time for banks to pay a fairer share.
‘At a time when the Chancellor needs to raise more revenue to support households and businesses through a looming energy bill crunch, Britain’s big four banks have made £200billion in profit since 2021. They can – and should – pay more tax.’
Banks’ profits have been boosted in recent years because of higher-for-longer interest rates , which have widened the gap between what they pay savers on deposits and charge borrowers for lending.
This gap – net interest income – is a key measure of profitability for lenders. For Barclays UK, it rose 6 per cent year-on-year to £2billion in the third quarter as the fallout from the Middle East war pushed interest rate expectations higher.
Income from both its UK retail and corporate banks increased, as well as from the wealth management and investment arms.
The investment bank, which makes up around 48 per cent of revenues, generated £3.1billion, boosted by trading volatility.
And income from equities soared 47 per cent to £689million, as traders continued to take advantage of the market changes as well as the latest moves in AI stocks.
Barclays' share price, which has suffered since news of the Chancellor’s tax plans, fell 2 per cent in early trading.
Venkatakrishnan said he was ‘pleased with the ongoing momentum of Barclays’ operational and financial performance’.
Healey declared banks a 'jewel in the crown of the British economy' and now he's looking to tap them for additional revenue.
Targeting the financial sector with higher levies comes with trade-offs, with concerns over the UK's competitiveness and its knock-on impact on economic growth.
Any increase to the banking surcharge could be passed on to consumers through higher mortgage rates and other loans, trade body UK Finance warned last month.
To protect their profit margins, domestic banks could raise their mortgage prices or offer less competitive rates on new deals.
A higher surcharge may limit flexibility and therefore lead to tighter lending criteria, making it more difficult for prospective buyers to secure a mortgage approval.
Savers could also be punished. Lenders may cut interest rates on savings accounts to try to recoup the lost revenue caused by higher taxes. Lower rates while inflation is rising means reduced real returns for savers.
Meanwhile, those who rely on dividend income from UK banks may also take a hit after the Budget if banks reduce shareholder payouts to cover the tax bill.

Employers continue to hold onto workers even as hiring remains weak, sending weekly jobless claims to around their lowest levels in records that stretch back nearly six decades.
Initial filings for unemployment insurance slipped to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ending Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
That marked another leg lower in the low-fire trend, with the total just off the 189,000 reported for the week of July 18 that was the lowest since September 1969. Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is down to 197,750.
Those numbers come against an uncertain backdrop for the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September and have averaged a gain of just 69,000 a month in 2026. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, an increase largely due to a sharp spike in labor force participation. Layoffs have remained modest, declining by 61,000 in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Sept. 29.
Over the prior 12 months, the layoff rate measured as a share of the total workforce fell to 1%, down 0.2 percentage point during the period. Job openings were relatively flat during the period.
"Despite extremely pessimistic views expressed in consumer confidence surveys regarding the economy overall, countless headlines describing job cuts from a variety of businesses, and the phantom job-stealing power of AI, the claims data suggests that labor market conditions are stable," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a client note.
The data comes during the reference week that the BLS uses to calculate the payrolls growth number. The September jobs report will be released Nov. 5.
Federal Reserve officials gather next week to issue their latest decision on interest rates . Policymakers in recent days have characterized the labor market as a source of general strength and focused more of their attention on the nettlesome inflation problem that has kept the pace of price increases well above the central bank's 2% target.
Markets expect the Fed to hold off on a rate hike in October but then to institute another quarter percentage point increase in December.

articles.title_zh: Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
articles.content_orig:
As European officials flag more trade restrictions, Beijing bristles at the idea it can be pushed into yielding to Brussels’ demands
In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.
Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.
It has resulted in an awkward, terse trade peace: an agreement that was supposed to defuse a trade war has led to both sides, rhetorically at least, hardening their positions. With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January.

articles.content_orig:
American Express is bringing Airbnb into its travel rewards platform.
The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring more than 1 million Airbnb listings to Amex's travel portal and allow cardholders to earn rewards when booking the stays. It does not currently allow members to redeem points to pay for Airbnb bookings.
The launch adds Airbnb rentals to Amex's hotel portfolio, which includes more than 3,400 properties across its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection programs.
Amex members with either the consumer or business Platinum card can also now apply their $600 annual lodging credit — previously called the hotel credit — to Airbnb's higher-end Luxe stays and take advantage of a new $250 statement credit on eligible Airbnb Experiences after making a Luxe booking.
"We're excited to bring more choice and flexibility to American Express Card Members with this exclusive partnership. Both of our companies exist to help people travel more and better, and this partnership helps people see more of the world by making travel more rewarding," said Juan David Borrero, head of partnerships at Airbnb, in a news release.
Membership points vary by card:
The changes come as competition among premium credit cards continues to ramp up.
Last year, American Express raised the annual fee on its premium Platinum card to $895. In turn, it's been investing in cardholder perks such as new lounges in airports and at big-ticket events and experiences as a way to attract more high-paying customers.
Earlier this month, it announced an expansion of its Centurion Lounges , with renovations coming to four existing lounges and new ones planned for Newark Liberty International Airport and London Heathrow Airport. The Newark lounge will be the largest in its network.
The partnership also comes as Americans continue to opt for travel and luxury experiences, even as prices for airfare, gas and hotels rise. Despite higher costs, more than half of Americans reported making no changes to their travel plans this summer , a recent study by travel insurance company Squaremouth found.

articles.title_orig: Horrifying video shows Mexican teen falling to her death from carnival ride
articles.title_zh: Horrifying video shows Mexican teen falling to her death from carnival ride
articles.content_orig:
A Mexican teenager died after falling from a carnival ride, with horrific video showing her flying out of her seat as the ride reached full speed.
Gabriela Rodriguez Tezoco, 18, died on Tuesday night following the accident at a festival in Los Cabos, Baja California Sur, local outlet Expreso reported .
Cell phone footage taken by another rider shows Tezoco plummeting to the ground from “The Pendulum,” a spinning ride at the Cabo San Lucas Traditional Festivals.
Other riders could be heard screaming as the teenager fell off while the ride kept spinning at high speed.
Emergency services rushed to treat Tezoco, who was taken to a nearby hospital, where she sadly died from her injuries early Wednesday morning.
“It is with deep sorrow that we report that the young woman who was injured in the incident that occurred in the amusement park area of ​​the Cabo San Lucas Traditional Festivals, and who was immediately transferred to receive medical attention, lost her life despite the efforts of the health personnel,” the Los Cabos City Council wrote on social media.
“The Pendulum” ride was closed in the wake of the incident while safety tests are carried out on it and the other attractions at the fair, Los Cabos mayor Christian Agundez told local reporters.
“Today, with the same spirit with which we come together to celebrate, we must come together to support Gabriela’s family. It could have been any one of us. You are not alone,” Agundez said during an appearance at a concert which was part of the festival.
An investigation has been opened both into the circumstances and to determine potential liability, the Baja California Sur State Attorney General’s Office reported on Wednesday.
So far, no arrests have been made, and no one responsible for the ride’s operation has been publicly identified.
Tezoco had just graduated this summer from the Baja California Sur College of Baccalaureate Studies.
“May your smile remain alive in our memory and may your memory always be a light that guides us,” the school said in a tribute.

articles.title_orig: Why Elon Musk wants to merge Tesla and SpaceX before Trump leaves office
articles.title_zh: Why Elon Musk wants to merge Tesla and SpaceX before Trump leaves office
articles.content_orig:
The world's richest man confirmed this week that Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a merger. Together, the companies are worth about $3.5 trillion (€3.1tn), making it potentially the biggest merger ever.
It would cap a string of deals tying Elon Musk's businesses together, and the goal is to complete it while Donald Trump is still the US president, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.
A merger between Tesla and SpaceX would be the latest chapter in a story that began a decade ago, when Musk started stitching his companies together.
In 2016, Tesla bought SolarCity , a solar panel installer run by his cousins, a deal that was only upheld by a Delaware court after years of litigation.
In March 2025, his AI start-up xAI swallowed X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, which Musk acquired for $44 billion (€39.1bn) in 2022.
In February this year, SpaceX absorbed xAI , in a deal that valued the rocket maker at $1 trillion (€890bn) and the AI firm at $250 billion (€222bn), ahead of SpaceX's initial public offering (IPO).
Four months later, SpaceX listed on the Nasdaq, raising $85.7 billion (€76.3bn) in the biggest stock market debut in history.
Seen together, the deals look like part of a long-running plan to fold Musk's businesses into one publicly traded group. Musk himself spoke of "more and more overlap" between Tesla and SpaceX on an earnings call in July.
On Tuesday, Musk told analysts on SpaceX's earnings call that both companies had set up committees of independent board members to study a merger. He called it "a good idea", while admitting he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield".
Musk argues that AI will decide where both companies go next.
They are already jointly developing Terafab , an AI chip factory in Texas, while Tesla's driverless cars and Optimus humanoid robots could benefit from the computing power SpaceX is racing to build, including planned data centres in orbit.
SpaceX posted its first quarterly profit since listing, earning $4.4 billion (€3.9bn) as revenue jumped 161%, but its capital spending reached $19.6 billion (€17.4bn) in the quarter, mostly on AI.
By contrast, a day later, Tesla reported that its net profit fell 43% to $787 million (€700mn) on flat revenue of $28 billion (€24.9bn), as deliveries slipped 2%. In a combined company, SpaceX's surging revenue could help offset Tesla's figures.
Merging the businesses would also allow Musk to run all their operations under one roof, moving engineers and resources between the companies without disclosures or lawsuits over related-party deals.
Control is another potential benefit.
Musk owns about 48% of SpaceX and holds more than 80% of its votes through special shares, but only about 20% of Tesla. Since 2024, Musk has said he is uncomfortable turning Tesla into an AI and robotics leader without at least 25% of the votes.
A merger could also make him richer, as his Tesla pay package treats many of its performance goals as achieved if certain types of mergers go through.
Reportedly, the aim is to announce a merger deal in the first half of 2027 and complete it before US President Donald Trump's term ends in January 2029, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.
Completing the deal while Trump is in office could give it a friendlier political reception, although it would still face regulatory and shareholder scrutiny.
Musk, who led Trump's cost-cutting drive in 2025 before a public falling-out , has since made up with the US president and returned to the administration.
He has also become the biggest known donor supporting Republican candidates in next month's US midterm elections, giving more than $276 million (€245mn) since July, according to a spokesperson for America PAC, Musk's conservative super PAC.
A Democratic win could bring tougher scrutiny of SpaceX's federal contracts and Tesla's self-driving software.
SpaceX itself warned in its listing documents that a shift in power in Congress could have a "material and adverse impact on our growth and competitive position".
The committees have yet to agree on terms, and any deal would need the backing of more than half of all Tesla shares, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle". He cautioned that a merger was not certain.
Tesla shareholders meet on 3 December.

articles.title_orig: Global Rush to Fix Security Flaw Uncovered by A.I. Leaves Sites Offline
articles.title_zh: Global Rush to Fix Security Flaw Uncovered by A.I. Leaves Sites Offline
articles.content_orig:
Government and company websites around the world briefly went dark and suspended some services, as operators scrambled to patch their systems after artificial intelligence helped find critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language.
Nearly three dozen UK government services are unavailable and four are “partially unavailable” while security upgrades take place, UK government minister Elizabeth Lloyd told the House of Lords Thursday. “No large public-facing critical services are being affected by the exercise but some limited services may temporarily be offline while security work is carried out,” a UK government spokesperson told reporters.
The US National Security Agenc y and Europe’s cybersecurity agency have advised companies to take immediate action to address two critical flaws in PHP, a programming language that powers 70% of all websites in the world, including WordPress and Drupal, an open-source content management system.
The PHP Foundation, the organization behind the coding language, has released a patch for the bugs, which have been hidden in their software for years, and is urging website operators to update their systems immediately.
Popular Irish news website The Journal was temporarily offline Thursday morning while it bolstered its “defences,” it said in a notice. The Journal is Ireland’s second most-used online news source, behind only RTÉ, the national broadcaster, according to the Reuters Institute.
The flaws in PHP – which originally stood for Personal Home Page – were uncovered by teams at OpenAI , Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz, and another cybersecurity company, Calif . The bugs, collectively called PHP2Shell, could allow attackers to hack into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords.
“With PHP behind such a vast share of the web, the exposure could reach almost everywhere people spend money online,” said Nigel Green, the CEO of deVere Group, a financial advisory firm.
“Booking platforms, marketplaces, subscription services, ticketing sites, delivery apps and utility portals could all be holding card details on systems built with the same kind of code,” he added.
Even world leaders urged organizations to take action. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that his cabinet was “closely monitoring the situation surrounding the vulnerabilities in PHP.”
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said companies should consider suspending services if necessary in order to reduce their exposure. “Please check if your publicly available websites use PHP, and prepare to apply the fix patch that will be released tonight… as soon as possible,” she posted on X Wednesday.
Japanese airline ANA, railway operator JR West and the country’s largest bank, MUFG, were among companies that reported some webpages and services temporarily suspended.
In Europe, government websites in France, Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands, including the Dutch cyber security agency, were temporarily taken offline while security fixes were implemented.
The Wikimedia Foundation, the non-profit that operates Wikipedia, told CNN Thursday that it was “in the process of addressing security vulnerabilities in PHP,” and that a number of its systems had been taken down as a “precautionary measure.”
AI played a crucial role in finding and fixing vulnerabilities “that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade,” according to Wiz, which said the episode marks an “AI inflection point.”
“What AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post Wednesday in which they described PHP as a “backbone of the web.”
“With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” they added.
The bugs were discovered in late August but were disclosed to the public only on Wednesday, after PHP had come up with a fix.
The flaws could allow attackers to remotely execute code, disrupt services and expose customer data, according to web infrastructure provider Cloudflare, which has been working with the PHP Foundation, Calif, OpenAI and Wiz to address the issue.
Researchers at Wiz used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, Wiz Atlas and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol during the research process.
Wiz researchers say the issue is on par with the Heartbleed bug from 2014, which impacted an encryption technology estimated to be used by two-thirds of the Web. Heartbleed allowed cybercriminals to access data that should have been protected.
Like Heartbleed, the researchers at Wiz say PHP2Shell could similarly serve as a turning point in cybersecurity. While the vulnerabilities existed for years, AI made it practical to deploy them.
“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” the researchers said.
“Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
– CNN’s John Liu, Anna Cooban, Amy Croffey and James Frater contributed reporting.
