articles.title_zh: Meta Offers Zuckerberg New Shares to Keep Him in California
articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg enters the debate on AI regulation, arguing against slowing down development. National Review columnist Caroline Downey analyzes his stance on safety oversight and independent evaluators.
Mark Zuckerberg has reached an agreement with Meta to remain in California after raising the possibility of leaving the state amid concerns over a proposed billionaire wealth tax.
Zuckerberg, Meta's CEO , previously told the company he was considering moving his primary residence outside California because of Proposition 40, a ballot initiative that would impose a one-time tax equal to 5% of net worth on billionaires who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026, if approved.
Under the agreement, Zuckerberg will receive non-voting shares that he could sell to help cover a potential wealth tax bill in exchange for a commitment to remain a resident of California , or the state where Meta maintains its headquarters, for eight years, according to Reuters.
Zuckerberg, the world's sixth-richest person with a net worth approaching $250 billion, according to Forbes, could face a substantial tax bill that might require him to sell company shares.
MARK RUFFALO CALLS GAVIN NEWSOM'S BILLIONAIRE TAX STANCE 'DISQUALIFYING' AHEAD OF CALIFORNIA VOTE
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reached an agreement with the company that could allow him to cover a potential California billionaire wealth tax bill while maintaining voting control, according to Reuters. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images / Getty Images)
If passed by voters in November, the tax would be due in 2027, although payments could be spread over five years at an additional cost. Real estate, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Zuckerberg can immediately sell 20% of the Class C shares he receives, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the company, potentially allowing him to pay the tax without giving up voting control, according to Reuters.
Meta said Wednesday that it planned to issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027 to help fund acquisitions and retain top talent while maintaining Zuckerberg's control of the company.
In a statement provided to FOX Business, Meta pointed to comments from Chief Financial Officer Susan Li, who said the new shares were designed to help the company raise capital, compensate employees and pursue acquisitions while preserving its existing voting structure.
REAGAN ECONOMIST WARNS BILLIONAIRE TAX WOULD â€˜DESTROYâ€™ CALIFORNIA
Supporters hold signs advocating for the Billionaire Tax Now coalition during a news conference in Los Angeles, California, on Monday, April 27, 2026. (Caroline Brehman/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
"We created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders," Li said during Meta's third-quarter earnings call.
Meta also said the decision followed a unanimous recommendation from a special committee of independent directors, which concluded that the new stock class would help finance the company's growth and preserve Zuckerberg's leadership.
According to a company filing, the committee emphasized the importance of Zuckerberg remaining in California to maintain close coordination with Meta's management and proximity to its Superintelligence Labs.
Although the ballot measure has been endorsed by the California Democratic Party, some prominent Democrats, including Gov. Gavin Newsom , have opposed it.
Economist Art Laffer, a former economic adviser to President Ronald Reagan, previously warned that the measure could accelerate an exodus of California's wealthiest residents.
META ORDERED TO PAY $25B AFTER JURY FINDS IT MISLED USERS ON DATA PRIVACY
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg could sell newly issued non-voting shares to help cover a potential tax bill if California voters approve a proposed billionaire wealth tax. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
"No one would want to go there to build their wealth only to be faced with this type of tax. It would cause an exodus of billionaires, which have not left California because the income taxes do not affect the billionaires much at all. This tax would really affect them," Laffer said.
California entrepreneur Eric Schiffer, chairman of the family office Patriarch and CEO of Reputation Management Consultants, previously told FOX Business that passage of the measure could prompt wealthy entrepreneurs to leave California.
"I think the impact of this passing in California is a giant sucking sound of all of these entrepreneurs being sucked out of California because they're just not going to want to stay," Schiffer said.
California's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) said "some billionaires" may decide to leave the state in response to the tax, potentially reducing the income tax revenue they generate.
The LAO also estimated that departures and other behavioral changes could reduce state income tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually. However, the office estimated that the wealth tax could generate tens of billions of dollars over several years.

articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Met Xi Jinping and Took Tesla FSD to China — Now His CFO Says Getting the Green Light for Unsup
articles.content_orig:
The logo of Tesla is displayed on a smartphone screen with the SpaceX logo in the background.
The world’s richest man has publicly backed a potential combination of SpaceX and Tesla in what could be the biggest merger in history.
On Tuesday, Elon Musk , the CEO and largest shareholder of both companies, said the electric vehicle maker and the rocket company had formed special committees at the request of shareholders to discuss the idea.
“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, ​and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” Musk told SpaceX investors on a conference call.
“I think it would be a good ​idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” he added.
The committees, which are made up of independent directors, would need to agree on the transaction terms of any deal before putting it to shareholders for a vote. Musk said his conflict of interest prevents him from participating in their discussions.
Musk has previously teased a Tesla-SpaceX merger. On a July 22 earnings call, Musk said there was “more and more overlap” between Tesla and SpaceX as the companies expand into artificial intelligence and robotics. Last week, Barclays analysts suggested that a merger could be announced before Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting in December.
Tuesday’s call was the first confirmation that the companies were formally exploring a combination.
A merger could create a company worth around $3.5 trillion , putting it among the world’s most valuable companies. It could also become the biggest merger ever by deal value, potentially surpassing SpaceX’s record-setting $250 billion acquisition of Musk-owned AI company xAI in February. SpaceX is currently valued at about $2 trillion, and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. A deal could also help propel Musk back into trillionaire ranks , depending on its terms and how investors value the combined company. Musk owns around 48% of SpaceX and 20% of Tesla.
The shares of both companies rose in after-hours trading on Tuesday. SpaceX, which went public in June, reported a quarterly net profit of $4.4 billion. Musk told investors he expects annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027.
Some analysts, however, have warned of regulatory and geopolitical hurdles, particularly in terms of Tesla’s Chinese operations and SpaceX’s U.S. defence work. Morningstar analysts said a merger could raise U.S. national security concerns involving the combined company’s supply chain. JPMorgan analysts also flagged regulatory approval in China as a potential stumbling block.
Any deal could also face congressional scrutiny, which could intensify if Democrats win control of either chamber in the coming midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers have previously questioned Musk over conflicts of interest and raised national security concerns about reported Chinese investments in SpaceX. Democrats have also challenged major acquisitions in the past on consumer protection grounds. In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D, Mass.) criticized SpaceX’s IPO, citing Musk’s concentrated voting power and weak investor protections—concerns that could resurface in a Tesla-SpaceX merger.
A merger could bring two of Musk’s biggest businesses under one corporate umbrella, making it easier for the companies to move investments and resources between projects. “This would allow him to run all their operations under one roof without tripping on as many governance issues,” wrote Morningstar analysts Seth Goldstein and Nicolas Owens in June. “For example, Musk could move Tesla software developers or engineers to work on SpaceX AI projects, and vice versa, or have Tesla and SpaceX supply one another without the need for related party transaction disclosures or risking shareholder lawsuits claiming the resources of one firm are being diverted for the benefit of the other.”
Analysts noted that Tesla’s robotaxis could benefit from Starlink connectivity, while its autonomous vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots could more closely integrate SpaceX’s AI technology. SpaceX’s planned orbital data centers, meanwhile, could potentially benefit from access to Tesla’s battery and energy storage products.
A combined company could also mean greater control of several stages of the AI value chain, from chip design and planned manufacturing to computing infrastructure, AI software, and its deployment in vehicles and robots.
The companies already collaborate. In March, they announced Terafab , a joint semiconductor manufacturing project intended to produce chips for Tesla’s vehicles and humanoid robots and SpaceX’s planned AI satellites. SpaceX technologies have also been used in some Tesla products, including the new Roadster prototype , which uses SpaceX-developed thrusters.
David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group, told the BBC that a merger also appears to align with Musk’s long-held ambition of colonizing Mars . Musk previously outlined plans to send Tesla’s Optimus robots to the planet aboard SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft.
A merger could also strengthen Musk’s influence over Tesla’s direction. Barclays estimated that a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla could give Musk around 37% of the combined company while controlling around 56% of its voting power. He currently controls around 82% of voting power at SpaceX and 20% at Tesla . That could represent either a benefit or a risk for shareholders, as decision-making would become faster but have fewer checks.
“One thing I don’t think people talk enough about with SpaceX and Tesla as well: You do still have a huge amount of key-man risk here,” wrote Morningstar analyst David Sekera earlier this month. “God forbid anything were to happen to Elon Musk.”

articles.title_zh: Space Debris Found Twice Within Days Amid ‘Growing Casualty Risk’
articles.content_orig:
Indonesia rocket debris? Image credit: BRIN
When it rains space debris.
Two cases of suspected Chinese rocket debris have been reported, in Indonesia and in the United States.
Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) reports that several bits of debris crashed into an oil palm plantation in Sampit, East Kotawaringin, Central Kalimantan.
BRIN researcher, Thomas Djamaluddin, said the object found on October 19 was a fragment of a Chinese ZhuQue-2E (ZQ-2E) rocket. There is a ZQE code associated with the ZhuQue-2E rocket, he adds.
There is a ZQE code associated with the ZhuQue-2E rocket. Image credit: BRIN
The rocket was developed by LandSpace, a Chinese commercial space startup and departed from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in China on October 14, 2026, carrying ten satellites.
Minnesota object. Image credit: Stevens County Sheriff’s Office
Yet another incident of possible space junk took place on October 14, 2026, at approximately 3:30pm, the Stevens County Sheriff’s Office in Minnesota received a phone call of foreign debris that was found in a cornfield in Scott Township.
“Upon responding, deputies confirmed that a large, metallic object, approximately 11-feet in diameter, presumably a space object, was present in the cornfield,” reports the sheriff’s office.
The Minnesota duty officer was notified of this and federal agencies responded.
“The Sheriff’s Office is working closely with several state and federal agencies to identify and notify the owner of the debris and to plan for removal from the field. Agency officials have determined that there is no danger to the public due to this incident,” the office stated in a press release.
In a twisted bit of irony, the Minnesota debris may also be associated with a LandSpace Zhuque-2E rocket. According to Ars Technica , it could be tied to the rocket’s upper stage, hardware launched from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on September 15.
In both cases – Sampit and Scott Township — the recovered fragments are being examined to help identify their origin.

articles.title_orig: Russia Pounds Kyiv in Overnight Missile and Drone Barrage – 1 Dead, 24 Injured, Including 4 Children
articles.title_zh: Russia Pounds Kyiv in Overnight Missile and Drone Barrage – 1 Dead, 24 Injured, Including 4 Children
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks on Kyiv killed one person and injured 24 others, including 4 children. Strikes damaged metro infrastructure on the South Bridge, an ambulance station, six emergency vehicles, homes and businesses.
Russian forces launched successive waves of ballistic missiles and attack drones against Kyiv overnight into Thursday, Oct. 22, killing one and injuring at least 24 people, including four children, and damaging a metro bridge, an ambulance station, residential buildings and civilian infrastructure across the Ukrainian capital.
Initially, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported in a Telegram update Thursday morning that the number of injured had risen from six to 15, including two 15-year-old children.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
However, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported at 7:55 a.m. that one person had been killed and 22 others injured, including four children, in Russian attacks on the capital.
In a statement issued at 9:21 a.m., the Kyiv City Military Administration said that 24 people had been injured, 16 of whom had been hospitalized.
Russian forces launched ballistic missile strikes on six districts of Kyiv starting on the evening of Oct. 21, causing fires and damage, the DSNS said:
Dniprovskyi district: One person was killed, and a child was hospitalized. Homes and vehicles were damaged, while residential and non-residential buildings caught fire. Five other people were injured.
Darnytskyi district: Transport infrastructure was damaged. No injuries were reported.
Sviatoshynskyi district: A non-residential building and a restaurant complex caught fire. The blaze, which covered 1,100 square meters, has been extinguished.
Obolonskyi district: Non-residential buildings were damaged, and fires broke out. Two people were injured. The fires have been extinguished.
Pecherskyi district: Buildings, ambulances and a monastery were damaged. Eight people were injured, including three children.
Holosiivskyi district: Six people were injured when a non-residential building was struck.
The overnight bombardment also damaged metro infrastructure on Kyiv’s  South (Pivdennyi) Bridge, prompting traffic restrictions on a key crossing over the Dnipro River.
In the central Pecherskyi district, Russian strikes damaged an ambulance station and six emergency medical vehicles, according to the mayor.
The latest attack marks another assault on essential civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, with Russian missiles hitting residential neighborhoods, transport facilities and emergency medical services.
The Russian bombardment also struck part of the capital’s metro infrastructure on the South Bridge, a major crossing connecting Kyiv’s two banks.
“As a result of the shelling, part of the metro infrastructure on the South Bridge was damaged,” Klitschko reported on Telegram .
The Kyiv City Military Administration announced traffic restrictions on the bridge in the direction from the right bank to the left bank because of the attack.
The bridge carries both road traffic and a section of Kyiv’s green metro line across the Dnipro.
Damage to the crossing adds pressure to Kyiv’s transport network as the capital faces repeated Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure.
Russian strikes also damaged an emergency medical facility in Kyiv’s Pecherskyi district.
Klitschko confirmed that the damaged building was an ambulance station and that six ambulances had also sustained damage.
No medical personnel were injured, the mayor said.
The damage to emergency medical services came as ambulances and rescue crews were responding to casualties elsewhere in the capital.
The overnight strikes also sparked a fire at a restaurant building in Kyiv’s Sviatoshynskyi district.
The Kyiv City Military Administration reported that the fire broke out following the Russian attack, adding another civilian site to the growing list of damaged properties.
Earlier Wednesday evening, Russian missiles struck residential buildings and businesses in Dniprovskyi district.
Klitschko reported direct hits on a vehicle repair workshop and a private residential building, while debris damaged another house.
Emergency crews were dispatched amid concerns that people could be trapped beneath the rubble.
At another location in the same district, missile debris fell near a gas station, causing additional damage.
In Darnytskyi district, a Russian strike hit the grounds of a transport infrastructure facility, according to the mayor.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued repeated warnings as Russian ballistic missiles approached the capital late Wednesday and after midnight Thursday.
The warnings began during Wednesday evening’s assault, when explosions were reported across Kyiv.
Further ballistic missile threats followed after midnight, including warnings shortly after 12 a.m. and another at approximately 12:31 a.m.
The Air Force also tracked Russian attack drones approaching the Kyiv region and subsequently warned of a drone over the capital.
The successive threats forced residents to remain in shelters as emergency crews responded to damage across multiple districts.
Russian forces launched a massive combined missile and drone attack against Ukraine beginning at 6 p.m. on Oct. 21, targeting Kyiv as the primary strike location, the Ukrainian Air Force reported.
The attack involved Iskander-M and S-400 missiles, Zircon and Oniks missiles, and 210 strike drones, including jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Gerbera and Italmas drones, and Parodiya (Parody) decoy drones.
“The primary target of the strike was Kyiv,” the report said.
The attack was countered by Ukrainian Air Force aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare (EW) and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
As of 9 a.m. on Thursday, preliminary data showed that Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 181 Russian drones, including 87 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Gerbera drones and other types.
“Ten strike drones remain in the air; combat operations are ongoing! Do not ignore air raid alerts!” the Air Force warned at 9.01 a.m.
Russian weapons struck 32 locations, while debris from intercepted drones fell at eight other locations.
The latest strikes came amid renewed US-led diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to Russia’s war against Ukraine.
On Wednesday, US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg after holding discussions with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European officials earlier in the week.
The Kremlin subsequently signaled willingness to resume trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US.
However, Moscow has not abandoned its territorial claims or its opposition to Ukraine joining NATO.
Meanwhile, Russian forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and essential infrastructure as winter approaches.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly stressed that any negotiated settlement must include reliable security guarantees to prevent renewed Russian aggression.

articles.title_orig: China's Stock Market Crashes 20%: 3 Reasons Why The Dragon Is Losing Its Fire
articles.title_zh: China's Stock Market Crashes 20%: 3 Reasons Why The Dragon Is Losing Its Fire
articles.content_orig:
China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.
The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.
Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment.
"I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.
Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.
The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.
Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.
China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.
Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC.
"For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.
While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities.
"It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.
Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

Oil prices climbed Thursday on worries over a possible escalation in the Middle East conflict as the U.S. reportedly plans to resume strikes against Iran.
Brent crude futures rose 2.68% to $111.74 a barrel as of 6:30 a.m. ET, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude gained 2.21% to $99.30.
The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, The New York Times reported, citing unnamed U.S. officials. Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.
The U.S. has also ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia.
State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets, after reports said that the U.S. had directed some staff in the wider Gulf region to leave.
The economic fallout from elevated oil prices, however, may be less severe than in previous decades, as consumers have become less vulnerable to energy shocks, according to David Wagner, head of equity and portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors.
"$100 oil today is very different than $100 oil, you know, 20, 30 years ago," Wagner said, noting that crude prices remain well below their inflation-adjusted historical highs.
He pointed to U.S. government data showing that gasoline accounted for roughly 5% of the average American's disposable income a decade ago, compared with about half that today, suggesting households may be better positioned to withstand elevated energy costs.
"I think we can hold that umbrella over our head ... from the rainstorm of oil," he said.

articles.title_orig: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for misleading Facebook users
articles.title_zh: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for misleading Facebook users
articles.content_orig:
A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after the company was found to have misled users about its privacy practices in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal .
The Wednesday ruling marks one of the largest-ever legal penalties for a tech giant — and just the latest court loss for Meta this year.
The company, then known as Facebook, disclosed in 2018 that the private information of as many as 87 million Facebook users was improperly obtained by political analytics firm Cambridge Analytica . The firm used that information to build profiles of American voters.
New Mexico sued Facebook in 2021, accusing it of mishandling state residents’ personal information and deceiving those users about its policies in connection with the incident.
A jury found in September that Meta had violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act more than 43 million times. State District Court Judge Francis Mathew criticized the company for what he described as a “coherent strategy designed to mislead the public” in his Wednesday penalty decision.
“Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model,” Mathew wrote.
After Wednesday’s penalty decision, Meta said it will appeal the decision and has accused New Mexico’s attorney general of conflating privacy and speech issues.
Meta agrees to pay $725 million to settle lawsuit over Cambridge Analytica data leak
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”
Meta’s legal battles threaten to strain its business, though court penalties and settlements remain relatively small compared to the company’s earnings so far.
The company reported earnings for the quarter ended in September on Wednesday, including lower quarterly profits than Wall Street had expected. It attributed the miss to a charge from the $18 billion multistate settlement it agreed to in August to resolve claims that its platforms have addicted and harmed young people.
New Mexico was not a party to that settlement, which also resolved the participating states’ outstanding claims related to Cambridge Analytica.
Meta posted income from operations of nearly $13 billion during the quarter, compared to nearly $23 billion that it said it would have earned without the settlement.
Meta settles landmark state child harm claims for $18 billion and promises changes to its platforms
Meta CFO Susan Li said on a call with analysts following the earnings report that the company is monitoring “active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” including additional youth-related trials set for later this year and next.
Meta was also ordered to pay nearly $1 billion in a separate New Mexico case earlier this year over claims that its platforms addicted and harmed young people. Meta, along with YouTube, also lost a case in March in Los Angeles brought by a young woman with similar addiction and harm claims. The companies plan to appeal.
Still, Meta’s business continues to grow at a strong clip thanks in large part to its investments in artificial intelligence. The company posted sales growth of 26% year-on-year to more than $64 billion in the quarter.
Meta’s stock ( META ) jumped more than 3% in after-hours trading following the report on Wednesday.
Meta launched its Muse AI personal assistant app in September. The app quickly rocketed to the top of app stores and has gained more than 10 million users, according to the company. It also launched its latest foundation model, Muse Wonder, last month.
The company said Wednesday that its AI investments are boosting its core advertising business “through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetization.” Its average price per ad, a key metric for the company, jumped 14% year-over-year in the September quarter.
Across the industry, tech companies face questions about their heavy spending on AI infrastructure. Meta’s capital expenditures during the quarter reached nearly $35 billion, up 80% from the year-ago quarter. And the company narrowed its full-year capital expenditure guidance to between $135 billion to $145 billion, the upper end of the range it had previously provided. Meta declined to provide spending guidance for next year.
But investors are signaling they’re willing to give Meta some leeway, given the success of Muse, said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com .
“The market has shifted from punishing Meta for spending to rewarding it for having a compelling product story,” Cohen wrote in emailed commentary.

articles.title_zh: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
articles.content_orig:
The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate, with three people killed in strikes across the country.
Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising in the past month.
The Houthis have responded to Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in Saudi Arabia. A recent strike on Riyadh's international airport was the deadliest in the kingdom in years.
"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.
The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".
In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.
No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.
The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule.
An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

The decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field is praised as "a welcome outbreak of common sense" in the Sun. But, in what is described as "Net Zero madness", the Daily Mail says the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is poised to reject plans for the Rosebank oil field. "Pathetic" is the paper's headline. A source tells the Times that it would be hard to justify approving the project on climate grounds. Another says Fahnbulleh has long been opposed to it. But, according to the Guardian, she "could still be overruled" by the prime minister, who "may hear different representations" from the chancellor.
John Healey gives clues about next week's Budget in an interview with the Times . He says that alleviating the cost of business is "in the end the only way to deal with people who have cost of living pressures". With the chancellor expected to cut regulations, a senior Treasury source likens them to "the sludge" which is "choking firms".
Separately, the Financial Times reports that Healey has suffered a "double blow" with increases in both inflation and government borrowing. One economist tells the paper the figures are "dismal" and signal that he will deliver a "cautious Budget that has little net impact on the economy and leaves the toughest fiscal decisions for next year".
Analysis by the Daily Telegraph suggests that Russia is using fishing vessels to spy on the UK's undersea cables. The paper says these could be attacked in any future war, potentially paralysing the country. A Nato source is quoted as saying: "We're absolutely aware of what Russian civilian fishing ships are up to and where... Some of them have never seen a single fish on their deck." Meanwhile, warnings about Britain's readiness for war are highlighted in the Daily Express , which calls for an increase in defence spending.
And a royal insider tells the Daily Mirror that Prince William "has no intention of engaging with" his brother, Prince Harry, who has called for reconciliation. The source says "there isn't a world where the Prince of Wales can imagine" a reunion. The headline is: "Ruled out."

articles.content_orig:
Sea mines have resurfaced as a threat in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran claimed Oct.17 that two oil tankers caught fire after striking the explosives, raising fresh alarms over the safety of one of the world's most critical shipping lanes.
This came as the International Maritime Organization (IMO) warned that sea mines pose a serious threat to vessels navigating the strategic waterway and while Tehran continues to maintain its own unauthorized shipping corridor inside its territorial waters.
"The traffic separation scheme, the information that we have is that they still have mines. And of course, whilst the conflict is ongoing, it's very difficult for us to use third parties to verify that it is clear of these hazards," IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez told Fox News Digital.
Inside The Dangerous Us Mission That Cleared Iran's Mines From Hormuz Shipping Lanes
Mine countermeasures ship USS Dextrous (MCM 13) (not pictured) sails with ships participating in the Oman-led exercise Khunjar Hadd in the Gulf of Oman. Dextrous is deployed to the U.S. 5th Fleet area of operations to help ensure maritime security and stability in the Middle East Region.
"So in the meantime, we cannot guarantee that a vessel that intends to transit that route will not be hit by a mine."
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy said Saturday that two oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported, citing Iran's official Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA).
State media also said both tankers were carrying about 2 million barrels of crude oil, according to Reuters .
IRNA also reported that the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and attempted to use a route through the strategic waterway that Iran had not authorized.
Iran Warns Ships Of 'Forceful Response' As Us-backed Hormuz Route Challenges Tehran's Grip
Smoke column rises from tanker El Gaia after incident in Strait of Hormuz
The second tanker was left immobilized after striking a mine, according to the Reuters report.
The alleged strikes came as Tehran continued to maintain its transit passageway inside Iranian territorial waters, imposing tolls and safety fees administered by the IRGC — a framework rejected by Washington and the IMO as inconsistent with international maritime law.
International shipping through the narrow chokepoint has historically relied on an IMO-approved traffic separation scheme adopted in 1968.
"Right now there's only one route that was adopted back in 1968 that is approved and recognized for IMO and that appears in all the charts for the vessels to operate," Dominguez explained.
Iran Fails To Strike Deal With Us As Deadline Passes And Trump Calls For 'White Flag Of Surrender'
Attacks on vessels around the Strait of Hormuz have surged over the past two weeks. Senior Iranian officials also told Reuters that Tehran has shifted its strategy for attacking commercial vessels during that period.
"There's only one route that should be used for transit, but it's not clear of mines right now, so it's not safe."
"We have received confirmation from Iran about the establishment of its temporary route in the waters," he added before stating that the route was not provided with "an official confirmation or a decision of the organization."
"Any other route needs to actually be sent to the organization to go through the processes, and we have not received that."
"We have received communication from Iran to use that route because of the conflict," Dominguez clarified.
"That's the way that it's been presented. But anything for us to approve needs to go through the mechanisms at the international maritime organizations and the member states need to review it."
The developments also came amid stalled negotiations between Washington and Tehran over ending the conflict and restoring maritime traffic.
Distress Call Captures Tanker Under Fire, Iran Shuts Hormuz Trapping Thousands Of Sailors
Basij paramilitary force speed boats are sailing along the Persian Gulf near a general cargo vessel
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a former Revolutionary Guard commander, said Tehran considered Washington's latest response to negotiations "insufficient," Reuters reported, according to IRNA.
Rezaei said the U.S. had accepted some of Iran's seven conditions but that other issues remained unresolved, adding that Tehran was no longer responding to Washington and that the U.S. needed to clarify the outstanding matters.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran had submitted a proposal to Washington through Qatar, which is mediating the negotiations, outlining conditions under which the Strait of Hormuz could reopen and normal maritime traffic resume within seven days.
"Our situation is clear and based on ⁠the seven-day proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which ​we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table ​and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said in ​Baghdad, Reuters reported
Iran Requests Talks With Us As White House Warns 'Violence Will Be Met With Violence'
As U.S.-Iran talks opened Sunday in Switzerland, a dispute over who controls and monitors billions of dollars in potentially unfrozen Iranian assets emerged
Meanwhile, attacks on commercial vessels around the Strait of Hormuz have surged over the past two weeks.
Senior Iranian officials also told Reuters that Tehran has shifted its strategy for attacking commercial vessels during that period.
For commercial shipping operators, Dominguez warned that the continued threat of mines and attacks means the waterway has yet to return to normal operations.
The Strait of Hormuz is "not open for business in the way that it was before the conflict started," he said.
"Our role right now is to prepare for when we have the opportunity to go back, resume the operations, follow all the procedures at IMO, but not until the root causes are addressed and those are beyond IMO."

Helen Haines, the Australian MP struck by a car outside her constituency office in an alleged attack on Monday, has had her second leg amputated, her husband has announced.
Addressing the media on Wednesday afternoon, Phil Haines said: “Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family.”
Surgeons on Monday had amputated Ms Haines’ left leg on Monday night after she was airlifted to hospital. The 65-year-old was struck twice by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta in Victoria .
A suspect identified as Brendan Nugent, 43 , faces three charges over the alleged attack on the Independent MP, as police consider bringing additional charges against him. He remained silent during his first court appearance earlier on Wednesday.
Providing an update to the media on behalf of their family, Mr Haines said his wife’s road to “recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter.
“She is a determined person who will do her best with our support and love to recover. And that is what we hope for.
“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person, incredibly supportive of all around her; her family, her community, anybody she comes across and her mind.
“We are grateful and thankful that, at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”
He said that the couple will celebrate their 40th anniversary in November and, in the last four months, have welcomed four grandchildren.
Thanking the public for the support that has been extended to the family, Mr Haines paid special tribute to first responders at the scene of the alleged attack on Monday, including police, paramedics and the members of the community.
“One thing I’ve learned in the last two days, reinforced by many people, is to take things day by day. I know it’s a cliche, but it’s a cliche for a very good reason.
“So I thank you all for being here. I thank you for listening. And please keep sending Helen your love and our family as well.”
Australia’s governor-general Sam Mostyn said she was “touched” to be invited by Mr Haines to attend the press conference, and also expressed gratitude towards the first responders.
She reiterated that Ms Haines’ recovery would be taken “day by day” after what she described as Monday’s “violent attack”.
She called on Australians to “do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack” and to “not descend into violence and chaos and division”.
The incident has shocked Australia , a country where political violence is rare and politicians have always been accessible to the public. Most MPs and even senior ministers go about their work and personal lives without being accompanied by security teams.
Prime minister Anthony Albanese, who characterised the attack as deliberate, called for a calming of political rhetoric in the wake of the incident, and thanked bystanders for intervening . He also spoke with local barber Ricky Jefferies, who helped detain the suspect .
